# Nibble

> A free, account-free pixel art and animation editor that runs entirely in the
> browser. This site is designed to BE USED BY AI agents, not to sell you AI.
> Nothing is sent to a server; there is no backend.

## How to use it as an agent

Open the editor page: /editor/

That page exposes a global object, `window.nibble`. The first call is always:

    window.nibble.help()

That call is a handshake: the site detects you, the UI switches to "Co-op Mode"
and the user sees a live ticker of everything you do. `help()` is not just an
API listing — it also returns advice based on the current canvas state.

Deeper topics:
help("drawing") | help("animation") | help("rig") | help("palette")
help("export") | help("project") | help("permissions")

## Golden rules

1. NEVER send pixels one at a time. Draw a whole sprite with one `drawFromText`
   call. Clicking pixel by pixel on a 32x32 canvas would be 1024 actions.
2. Wrap multi-step work in `beginBatch("label")` / `endBatch()` so the user can
   undo everything you did with a single Ctrl+Z.
3. Call `readCanvas()` to see what you drew. It returns exactly the format you
   write, so you can check and correct yourself without screenshots.
4. Read the `hint` field on every return value — the site actively coaches you.
5. A denied call is an answer, not an obstacle. Do not look for a way around the
   permission system; ask the user to grant the scope and retry.
6. To animate, name the moving parts once and move them by name. See the rig
   section below — it is the difference between one call and a thousand.

## The rig: name the parts, then move them by name

This is the highest-leverage part of the API and the reason Nibble exists in
this shape. Redrawing a sprite once per frame is the most expensive way to
animate. Instead, name a chunk of the sprite once:

    nibble.definePart({
      name: "left_leg",
      x: 12, y: 24,                        // the handle
      box: { x: 10, y: 22, w: 5, h: 8 },   // the pixels it carries
    })

From then on you speak in parts, not pixels:

    nibble.movePart("left_leg", 0, -2)     // handle AND pixels, one undo step
    nibble.flipPart("left_leg", "x")       // lossless
    nibble.rotatePart("left_leg", 90)      // 90° multiples lossless
    nibble.recolorPart("left_leg", { to: "#b13e53" })

Key the poses and let Nibble fill in the frames between them:

    nibble.addFrame({ copyFrom: 0 })
    nibble.movePart("left_leg", 0, -3)
    nibble.setActiveFrame(0)
    nibble.tween({ count: 2 })

`setPartHandle(name, x, y)` moves the handle WITHOUT the pixels — that is how
you key a pose you want to interpolate towards. `defineBone({name, from, to})`
records that two parts are attached; it draws a line and gives you structure to
reason about. `describeRig()` tells you which parts are still missing a handle
or a box.

tween() does TRANSLATION ONLY — no squashing, bending or mesh warping. Pixel art
turns to mud when you deform it, so this is deliberate, not a limitation to work
around. Expect to touch up in-betweens by hand where it matters. If the parts
only travel a pixel or two, the in-betweens land on the same pixels and the
return value says so.

## Permissions

The user owns a set of switches. Every call is checked against them.

    draw         on  by default   paint, flood fill, clear the current frame
    animate      on  by default   frames, fps, playback
    layers       on  by default   add / show / hide / lock / rename layers
    palette      on  by default   change the project palette
    destructive  OFF by default   resize, newProject, deleteFrame, deleteLayer
    files        OFF by default   downloads, loading images from a URL

A denied call returns `{ ok: false, error, hint, deniedScope }` — it does not
throw. The editor simultaneously shows the user a request they can approve.

Call `getPermissions()` at any time to see what you are currently allowed to do.

Things that are deliberately NOT in the API: the user's saved drafts, storage,
settings, and any file system access. There is no way to list, open or delete
the user's other projects.

## Limits

    rate limit          120 calls per 10 seconds
    drawFromText        max 4096 rows, 4096 characters per row, 512 legend keys
    setPixels           max 250 000 pixels per call
    canvas              max 512 x 512
    part box            max 2048 x 2048 (a box is a pixel buffer, so it is capped)
    importImage         data:, blob: and same-origin paths are free; anything
                        that resolves to another origin needs "files" - and the
                        check runs on the RESOLVED url, so obfuscating the
                        scheme does not get you past it

Everything you do lands in the undo history as a single step per call (or per
batch), so the user can always take it back.

## Typical flow

    nibble.help()
    nibble.usePalette("sweetie-16")
    nibble.beginBatch("bouncing slime")
    nibble.drawFromText({
      rows: ["..DDDD..", ".DLLLLD.", "DLWLLWLD", ".DDLLDD."],
      legend: { D: 7, L: 6, W: 12 },
      x: 12, y: 10
    })
    nibble.addFrame({ copyFrom: 0 })
    nibble.setPixels([{ x: 12, y: 11, c: 6 }])
    nibble.setFps(10)
    nibble.endBatch()
    nibble.readCanvas()

`legend` values are either palette indices (numbers) or hex strings such as
"#ff0044". The character "." means transparent.

## Pages

- /            landing page, what Nibble is
- /editor/     the editor — this is where window.nibble lives
- /agent/      human- and agent-readable API reference

## Facts worth knowing

- Valid FPS values are 5, 10, 12.5, 20, 25, 50 — exactly the ones where 100/fps
  is a whole number of centiseconds, which is the unit GIF stores frame delay in.
  (12.5 fps is 8 cs. 60 fps would be 1.67 cs and the animation would drift, so
  setFps(60) rounds to 50 and tells you so.)
- Layers are global to the project (the Aseprite model), not per frame.
- Exports: PNG, animated GIF, animated APNG, sprite sheet with Aseprite-compatible
  JSON that Godot and Unity importers read directly, and a .nibble project file.
- exportGif() is limited to 256 colours and 1-bit alpha; exportApng() has neither
  limit and is lossless. Prefer APNG when the sprite has soft edges or many colours.
- Rig parts are written into the sprite sheet JSON as Aseprite "slices" (name +
  per-frame bounds + pivot), so the names you choose survive the export.
- The editor UI is bilingual (Turkish / English). This API is English only.
